RagShortTexts: Vague feudal boundaries across Gascony and Guyenne remain a powder keg between England and France.

Variants.Content: Henry III held Gascony as a fief of the French crown under the Treaty of Paris of 1259, which settled a long dispute by making the English king a vassal rather than a sovereign rival. The treaty did not draw clean lines on the ground. Anglo-Gascon bastides, planned towns founded along the rivers, faced French royal provosts who claimed the right to hear cases and levy customs. Every toll on river traffic and every disputed land grant gave both sides a reason to send letters, lawyers, and armed men. Jurisdiction in Gascony stayed uncertain for decades, and the boundary between English and French authority was contested in courts and on the road alike.

Bordeaux wine had to flow down the Gironde to English ports, and each toll post along the river took its cut. A baron with vineyards or river tolls watched royal bailiffs closely. When French officers arrived in Gascony, local lords weighed whether London or Paris would confirm their charters and protect their customs, and sealed letters from both courts arrived by the same couriers.
Nobles argue over Latin parchments, but common folk pay the toll in every grape harvest. As soon as the French bailiff departs, the Duke's collectors arrive to inspect our cellars.
